title: UN climate summit may have ended in failure, but momentum for fossil fuel deal is growing
summary: A coalition of countries has decided that rather than accept a bad deal, they will meet on their own, separately, outside the UN process to tackle the problem amongst their like-minded allies.

image.caption: A demonstration at COP31 in Turkey, where climate talks broke down last week. (Khalil Hamra/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Science
A coalition of countries has decided that rather than accept a bad deal, they will meet on their own, separately, outside the UN process to tackle the problem amongst their like-minded allies.
Despite lack of deal at COP31, analysts say momentum growing for action on fossil fuels

Canadian climate campaigner Tzeporah Berman has been to a lot of UN climate conferences, waiting for a long time for the summits to actually address the central cause of the climate crisis: burning fossil fuels.

It took until the summit's 26th year — at COP26 in 2021 in Glasgow — for countries to agree to a final text that even mentioned oil, gas and coal. It took until COP28, in the United Arab Emirates, for countries to further acknowledge they will have to transition away from fossil fuels. And it took until this year, at COP31 in Turkey, for disagreement over fossil fuels to cause a complete breakdown in talks, with no agreement reached for the first time since 2009.
"In some ways, it's long overdue," said Berman, founder of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative, which seeks to build global agreement on ending the use of oil, gas and coal.
"You know, we've had 31 COPs dancing around the issue of fossil fuels. We talk about reducing emissions, but we don't talk about reducing production."

To Berman, the fault lines made clear in this year's negotiations could build momentum around another process away from the influence of countries that will defend their fossil fuel industries "no matter what."

This separate movement, bolstered by a series of nations that have announced their own plans to transition away from fossil fuels, could become "a companion to the Paris Agreement," she said, setting up a new global framework through trade, tax and debt measures to help countries end their use of oil, gas and coal.

"Every major treaty breakthrough in history — landmines, nuclear weapons, chemical weapons — were built by coalitions of the willing, not like a vote at the UN General Assembly with 190 countries," Berman said.

Ireland's environment minister, Darragh O'Brien, at the emotionally charged closing session of the COP31 summit, where delegates like him refused to accept a watered-down deal. (Khalil Hamra/The Associated Press)
Why is a fossil fuel transition deal important?
Producing and burning fossil fuels for energy is responsible for about 75 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions — mostly carbon dioxide, but also other potent heat-trapping gases like methane.

With the world now set to overshoot 1.5 C of warming above pre-industrial levels, and well on its way to even more destructive heating levels without urgent emissions reductions, many countries are realizing that addressing fossil fuels directly is becoming important.

But it's not an easy task. Fossil fuels are also central to the world’s energy system. Oil, gas and coal together account for 79 per cent of global energy demand — to fuel transportation, industries, power plants and more.
Piles of coal near an industrial facility in China. (Ng Han Guan/The Associated Press)

It also means fossil fuel industries have a huge economic footprint in many countries, says Matthew Webb, clean power diplomacy expert at the energy and climate think-tank E3G. Across Asia, for instance, 80 per cent of coal power generation plants are under 20 years old, according to the International Energy Agency.

"Now, they can run for 40 to 50 to 60 years under sort of normal conditions," Webb said. Replacing those coal plants with renewables will hit the owners of those plants as well as the millions of people whose livelihoods depend on coal mining and operating those plants.

blocks.text: Yet a transition will be needed. If these coal plants are allowed to operate for their typical lifetimes under normal conditions, they will end up putting 330 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, according to the IEA.
That's more than the historical emissions to date of all coal-fired power plants that have ever operated in the world, something an already overheated planet can ill-afford.
Who will lead the transition?
In April, a group of 57 countries, including Canada, gathered in Santa Marta, Colombia, for the world’s first summit on transitioning away from fossil fuels.
The hosts — Colombia and the Netherlands — deliberately did not invite major emitters such as China, Russia and the U.S. to avoid the lengthy debates and roadblocks at UN conferences.

The Colombia meeting was not supposed to lead to any binding global agreements. But it established programs to identify fossil fuel subsidies, find solutions to debt and finance-related roadblocks to ending the use of fossil fuels, and support trade measures that encourage decarbonization.
It also led to the announcement of a new science panel, consisting of some of the world's top climate researchers who will advise countries in the energy transition.

Since then, several major economies have announced their plans to phase out fossil fuels — not just reduce emissions — and replace them with cleaner sources, such as France, Germany and Brazil. The next edition of this conference will be in July in Tuvalu, a small Pacific island nation that could disappear altogether due to rising sea levels.
Canada's 'difficult space'

In a statement, a spokesperson for federal Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin said that Canada stands by the commitment to transition away from fossil fuels that was made at COP28 in the U.A.E. in order to reach net-zero emissions by 2050.
At the latest summit, "Canada supported text that recognized this commitment," wrote Amy Faulkner.
However, "Canada has not finalized specific details for participation" for future conferences on transitioning away from fossil fuels, such as the one in Tuvalu.

Pratishtha Singh, international diplomacy expert at Climate Action Network Canada, a campaign group, said many of these countries' plans "need work" around whether they will actually put enough money and resources to support the transition.

She said that while Canada does not have its own roadmap for getting off fossil fuels, it was encouraging to see it attend. "Because for them it's a difficult space given the doubling down on fossil fuel infrastructure here at home. But they did show up in the conversations."

blocks.text: Webb says further talks on fossil fuel transition reflects "what’s going on actually in the real world" in terms of the growth of renewable energy like solar and wind, led by China, which is now the world leader in manufacturing solar panels and clean technologies like electric vehicles.
"We've actually got the capacity to build the solar panels we need, the wind turbines we need, and it is in part due to what China's done to restructure its economy," he said.
"We can make enough kit now to get to a safe climate."
